title: What tefillin are (Deuteronomy 6:8)
hookLine: two small leather boxes holding Torah passages, bound on arm and head for weekday morning prayer

lines: A BLACK BOX ON THE FOREHEAD.
cards: Maybe you've seen it in a photo, on a street corner, or at an airport gate early in the morning: someone standing quietly, a prayer shawl over their shoulders, a black leather strap wound around their forearm in neat coils, and a small black box right at the top of their forehead.
It can look strange if you've never seen it, even a little severe. But ask the person, and many will tell you it's the most intimate part of their day.
For the next five days, i'll open up this one practice, piece by piece.

teach.b: They're called tefillin, a word usually connected to tefillah, prayer. In English they're sometimes called phylacteries, from a Greek word meaning safeguards, but most Jews just say tefillin.
They come from a verse you already know, from the Shema: "And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for frontlets between thine eyes." Bind what? The words of God.

The rabbis read the verse literally: write the words down and tie them on. So there are two boxes of black leather, perfectly square, each with a leather strap. One is bound on the arm, one on the head.
Inside are tiny parchment scrolls, handwritten by a trained scribe with a quill and special ink.
They hold four Torah passages: two from Exodus, about remembering the Exodus, and two from Deuteronomy, including the Shema itself. So the verse that says bind these words is itself inside the box.
In the head box, the four passages are on four separate scrolls, in four compartments. In the arm box, all four are on one scroll, in one compartment.
Tefillin are put on for weekday morning prayer.

teach.h: FOR A SIGN UPON THY HAND.
teach.b: Not on Shabbat or major festivals, because those days are themselves a sign, the rabbis said, and don't need another.
Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, archaeologists found tefillin and their tiny parchments, two thousand years old.
And the rabbis taught great care: tefillin are never dropped, they're kept in a bag, and if one falls, many people kiss it when they pick it up.

how: Many Jews put on tefillin each weekday morning for the morning service, binding one box on the upper arm and one on the head, with blessings. They are not worn on Shabbat or major festivals.

practice: Choose one thing you want to remember all day, a promise, a person, a value, and put it into a few words. If you have a thread, a hair tie or a rubber band, put it on your hand; if not, press your thumb to one finger.
Let the body carry the reminder, so the mind doesn't have to.
